trait_value_raw: Cibotium comprises c. 9 species: 4 in the Hawaiian Islands, 2 in Mexico and N Central America, and 3 in Asia from NE India, S China and the Ryukyu Islands (Japan) to Malesia

The golden hairs on the rhizome and young parts of several Cibotium species have long been used in China and SE Asia as a styptic to stop bleeding (Praptosuwiryo, PROSEA 15, 2 (2003) 79)
All Cibotium species have ornamental value.

On slopes and stream banks in lowland rain forest from 60 m altitude to lower montane forest up to 1670 m or in rocky places on quartzite ridges, sandstone and granite cliffs (but not on calcareous soils), and on open, bare earth banks and paths recently cut through forest
Holttum (1963) stated that the species probably spreads by invading landslides.

Lowry (Malay. Nat. J. 23 (1970) 174) recorded trade of golden chicken plants (the apex of rhizome with rolled croziers and long brown hairs resembles a chicken) in Kuala Lumpur and Petaling Jaya, Selangor, in the late 1960s when the Genting Highlands development began
Currently, golden chicken plants are sold at several roadside stalls from Tapah to Cameron Highlands (Pahang)
Golden chicken plants are sold either in dry form as table ornaments or fresh for home gardening because the cut apex will grow when planted in the ground (Temiar collector, pers. comm.)
Collection of this plant for sale does not so far seem to impact on the population because, according to the Temiar collector, plants can still easily be found in sufficient quantity close by
In Asia, including Peninsular Malaysia, the hairs on the rhizome have long been used to staunch bleeding wounds (Praptosuwiryo, 2003)
Bidin (Paku-pakis Ubatan di Semenanjung Malaysia (1985) 58) stated that the young leaves are eaten as ulam (raw leaves eaten with pounded chillies and taken with rice).
It is not certain whether this species is completely trunkless

The specimen label of Ridley 5176 from G. Jerai reported the plant had a trunk ‘four feet tall’ and in Java, Backer & Posthumus (Varenflora voor Java (1939) 23, fig. 7) described the species as having a trunk
However, none of the wild plants observed by Holttum had a trunk, nor did the very old cultivated plants in Singapore Botanic Garden (Holttum, 1968)
All living plants and herbarium specimens collected since in Peninsular Malaysia have not been reported as having a trunk

In the 13th to 17th century, Cibotium barometz was believed to be the “Vegetable Lamb of Tartary” (also called the Scythian lamb), hence its species epithet, because the densely hairy apex of rhizome with four croziers when inverted resembles a woolly lamb (Holttum, 1968)
According to legend in Europe, a Scythian lamb is attached to the stem of a plant that would bend down so that the lamb could browse on the surrounding vegetation
Both the plant and lamb would die once all the vegetation was eaten.
